official_title: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget. Question: Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city's discretionary budget? Summary: Currently, Mayor works with City Administrator, bureaus, and community to develop proposed budget; Council then considers, amends as needed and adopts following public hearings. If measure is not approved, this process would not change. If measure approved, amended Charter would require Council to allocate an amount equivalent to at least 2% of the city's adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses (Council may identify funding from entire city budget to meet funding obligation) towards a participatory budgeting program that is: Developed with input from oversight committee, selected by a process determined by Council, of residents from all Council districts; Open to any resident's funding proposals for citywide or district projects: Proposals assessed and refined into limited number of feasible projects by city staff and budget delegates from all districts in a transparent process; Feasible projects advance to binding selection process open, accessible to all residents; Operational July 2027; Under recent forecast, preliminary estimate: 16.4 million in FY 2027-28; 17.0 million in FY 2028-29; Compliant with Oregon Local Budget Law. Other provisions.
plain_summary: Writes a 'participatory budgeting' program into Portland's charter. Every year the City Council would have to set aside an amount equal to at least 2% of the city's General Fund discretionary ongoing spending (about $16.4 million in the first year) for projects that residents propose and then pick in a binding vote. It starts July 2027. It adds no new tax, so the money would come out of the existing city budget.
yes_means: Portland must set aside about $16 million a year (at least 2% of discretionary spending) for projects that residents propose and choose by vote, written into the charter.
no_means: The budget process stays as it is: the mayor proposes a budget and the elected City Council amends and adopts it after public hearings.
current_law: The mayor works with the City Administrator, city bureaus and the public to write a proposed budget. The City Council then holds hearings, amends it and adopts it. There is no required set-aside for resident-chosen projects.
fiscal_impact: The ballot title's preliminary estimate is $16.4 million in fiscal year 2027-28 and $17.0 million in 2028-29. The measure creates no new revenue, so the money would be moved from other city spending; the Council may take it from anywhere in the city budget. The Yes campaign estimates running the program would cost about $1 million to $1.5 million a year. No city explanatory statement was filed.
confusing_wording_note: Three things to know. (1) In the county Voters' Pamphlet, one statement labeled 'Argument in Favor' (furnished by Max Steele) is satire that actually argues against the measure, so read the text, not the label. (2) '2%' sounds small, but it is about $16 million a year, and it is written into the charter, so only another citywide vote can change or end it. (3) The measure leaves key rules for later: who counts as a resident, the minimum age, how votes are cast and how budget delegates are picked are not spelled out. Supporters say that leaves room to design it well; opponents say it is too vague.

supporters_case.text: The Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX campaign says a record 78,743 Portlanders signed to put it on the ballot, that it does not raise taxes, and that it gives residents a direct say over how about $16 million a year is spent. Supporters point to participatory budgeting in New York, Boston and Metro's parks grants, and say it rebuilds trust in City Hall. Pamphlet supporters include the Multnomah County Democrats, Portland DSA, Sierra Club, Working Families Party, five Metro councilors and Healthy Democracy.

opponents_case.text: Opponents say the city just closed a $170 million shortfall and laid off about 100 workers, so a permanent $16 million set-aside with no new revenue means cuts to fire, police, 911, parks or shelters. They say unelected committees would make binding spending choices and that no U.S. city locks a set percentage into its charter. Pamphlet opponents include Mayor Keith Wilson, five city councilors, the fire and police unions, the Northwest Oregon Labor Council, the Taxpayers Association of Oregon and Portland Realtors.

official_title: Bonds to Increase Safety, Security; Repair, Construct Schools; Increase Accessibility. Question: Shall District issue bonds, projected to maintain 2026 bond rate, to increase safety, repair, replace aging schools and increase accessibility? If the bonds are approved, they will be payable from taxes on property or property ownership that are not subject to the limits of sections 11 and 11b, Article XI of the Oregon Constitution. Summary: This measure is projected to maintain District's 2026 bond levy rate of $1.62/$1,000 of assessed value. If passed, District will receive $8,168,000 in state matching funds. Reynolds School District seeks approval for a principal amount of $162.5 million in bonds to finance capital costs, including: Replace Aging Glenfair Elementary: Replace the 72-year-old school, which is overcrowded, has building systems beyond repair, contains hazardous materials, and has outdated safety & security measures. Replacement estimated to cost less than renovation. Repair Failing Infrastructure: Roofing, HVAC, plumbing, electrical systems, water heater replacement districtwide. Safety & Security: New fire alarm systems, PA systems, perimeter security across the district. Accessibility: ADA upgrades including accessible parking, sidewalks, ramps districtwide. Additional Projects: New turf field, bleachers at Reynolds High School. Requires community oversight committee, regular audits. Financials: Bonds may be issued in multiple series, each maturing within 21 years from issuance. No increase to 2026 bond levy rate of $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value expected. Actual bond levy rate may differ due to interest rates, changes in property value.
plain_summary: Only for Portlanders who live in the Reynolds School District, a slice of outer East Portland (most Portland homes are in other school districts). Lets the district borrow $162.5 million, repaid from property taxes, to replace 72-year-old Glenfair Elementary, fix roofs, heating and plumbing, add fire alarms and security, and make schools more accessible. The district says the tax rate would stay at today's $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value, and passing unlocks $8.2 million in state matching money.
yes_means: The district can borrow $162.5 million for school repairs, security and a new Glenfair Elementary, repaid by a property tax projected to stay at $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value.
no_means: The district does not get this new borrowing or the $8.2 million state match, and these projects would need another vote or other money.
current_law: Reynolds School District serves more than 9,000 students in 16 schools in Fairview, Troutdale, Wood Village and parts of Gresham and Portland. Its 2026 bond tax rate is $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value.
fiscal_impact: $162.5 million in general obligation bonds, issued in series that each mature within 21 years. Estimated rate $1.62 per $1,000 of assessed value, the same as the 2026 bond rate; actual rate may differ with interest rates and property values. The district would receive $8,168,000 in state matching funds only if it passes.
confusing_wording_note: Supporters call this a 'renewal' that 'does not raise your taxes.' That means the tax rate is projected to stay the same as today, not that nothing new is approved: it is $162.5 million of new borrowing repaid from property taxes for up to 21 years. Check your ballot: only Portland addresses inside the Reynolds School District see this measure.

supporters_case.text: The Reynolds School Board, which voted unanimously to refer it, and the district's principals say aging roofs, heating and plumbing are failing, fire alarms need replacing, and Glenfair Elementary is cheaper to replace than repair. They stress the rate stays the same and that passing brings $8.2 million in state matching money.

opponents_case.text: No arguments in opposition were filed in the county Voters' Pamphlet.
